content: 1. Lamivudine is an antiviral medication classified as a nucleoside analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor, approved by the FDA for the treatment of HIV-1 infection. 2. The drug carries a Black Box Warning, indicating significant risks associated with its use. 3. Common adverse reactions to lamivudine include headache, nausea, malaise, fatigue, nasal symptoms, diarrhea, and cough. 4. For adults with HIV-1 infection, the recommended dosage is 300 mg daily or 150 mg every 12 hours, in combination with other antiretroviral agents. 5. For adults with chronic hepatitis B (HBV) infection, the recommended dosage is 100 mg daily. 6. Pediatric patients aged 2 to 17 years with chronic HBV infection should receive 3 mg per kg once daily, up to a maximum of 100 mg daily. 7. Lamivudine is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to the drug or any of its components. 8. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with lamivudine and other nucleoside analogues. 9. 10. Treatment should be discontinued in patients who develop clinical or laboratory findings suggestive of lactic acidosis or significant hepatotoxicity. 11. In patients co-infected with HIV-1 and HBV, discontinuation of lamivudine may lead to post-treatment exacerbations of hepatitis, which can be severe or fatal. 12. Lamivudine-resistant HBV variants have been observed in both HIV-1-infected and non-HIV-1-infected patients, leading to diminished treatment response. 13. Lamivudine should not be used concurrently with other lamivudine-containing products or emtricitabine-containing products. 14. Ribavirin may reduce the phosphorylation of lamivudine, and co-administration with interferon alfa has been associated with hepatic decompensation in some HIV-1/HCV co-infected patients. 15. Lamivudine should be used cautiously in pediatric patients with a history of pancreatitis or significant risk factors for its development. 16. Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported in patients receiving combination antiretroviral therapy, including lamivudine, and may necessitate further evaluation and treatment. 17. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat, such as central obesity or peripheral wasting, has been observed in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy, though the mechanism and long-term consequences are unknown. 18. Lamivudine pharmacokinetics have been studied in both pregnant and non-pregnant women, showing similar profiles. However, its use during pregnancy should only occur if the potential benefits justify the potential risks to the fetus. 19. Lamivudine is excreted into human breast milk, and breastfeeding is not recommended for HIV-1-infected mothers due to the risk of postnatal transmission and potential adverse reactions in nursing infants. 20. In elderly patients, renal function should be monitored, and dosage adjustments should be made accordingly, as lamivudine is primarily excreted by the kidneys. 21. There is no known antidote for lamivudine overdose. Supportive treatment and monitoring are recommended in such cases. 22. Lamivudine is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, with an absolute bioavailability of approximately 86%. 23. The active metabolite of lamivudine, lamivudine triphosphate (3TC-TP), inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by causing DNA chain termination. 24. Lamivudine is a synthetic nucleoside analogue with activity against both HIV-1 and HBV, and its molecular formula is C8H11N3O3S. 25. The drug is predominantly eliminated via active renal secretion, and potential interactions with other drugs eliminated through the same pathway should be considered.
